q1: No, not reliably. Rolling-VAR connectedness rose over the year before 3 of 7 bear-market peaks (placebo p = 0.47; TVP-VAR p = 0.26). The smallest of the 14 pre-peak p-values is 0.04 (TCI rolling 250d, 63-day window), and after Benjamini-Hochberg correction the smallest q-value is 0.36: a hint of a rise in the last three months, not evidence of a systematic build-up. Connectedness does rise with the crisis itself: over the 63 days after the peak TCI rolling 250d (+1.53, p = 0.02), Dynamic TCI 500d (+0.31, p = 0.00), Absorption 250d (+0.01, p = 0.01). It is a volatility-state variable: alone it predicts next-quarter volatility (Newey-West t 2.9 to 3.3), but once today's realized volatility and VIX are controlled for, the t-statistics fall to 0.1 to 1.0. Out of sample, adding connectedness to a VIX / realized-vol / momentum model does not improve the prediction of a >=10% fall within three months (AUC 0.55 -> 0.42; difference 90% interval -0.29 to +0.03).
q2: In the standard Diebold-Yilmaz sense the transmitters are equities: EFA, SPY, EEM, IWM have the largest NET (+16 to +30 points) and are net transmitters in 94-100% of rolling windows. But 90% of the equity NET comes from same-day correlation, which is symmetric and only says these assets are central. Lagged spillovers carry the directional (predictive) content, and they are small: 2.6% of total connectedness in the macro network and 1.4% in the synchronous one. Their direction tracks how late each series absorbs equity news (Spearman -0.46 between that lag and lagged NET; the close hour alone gives 0.01 because it misses stale marks), and with synchronous prices no asset's lagged NET exceeds 1.9 points. In the tails, VIX, SPY, IWM have the largest Delta-CoVaR out-strength (descriptive). Which asset 'transmits' therefore depends on the definition, and none of these measures identifies a causal transmitter.
q3: On the descriptive evidence, XLRE Real estate (XLRE), ITB Homebuilders, IYR Real estate, XLU Utilities have the most negative rate betas holding the market fixed, and the lowest betas in the positive stock-bond-correlation (inflation) regime are ITB Homebuilders, XLRE Real estate (XLRE), IYR Real estate. At the other end, XLF Financials, XLE Energy, KRE Regional banks gain relative to the market when yields rise. The causal question, what a policy-driven rate rise does, is answered for the market as a whole but only coarsely by sector. FOMC days raise the variance of the 2Y yield 2.0x relative to control days (90% CI 1.6-2.5; 1.9x outside the zero lower bound). That is enough to identify the S&P 500's response, -0.98% per +10bp policy-driven 2Y move (90% CI -2.07 to -0.33), but only 3 of 18 sector responses relative to the market have a 90% interval excluding zero (Discretionary -0.48%, Comm. services -0.32%, Growth (R1000G) -0.18%). The point estimates rank ITB Homebuilders, XLY Discretionary, XLC Comm. services as most hurt by hawkish surprises.
q4: Yes. 5 of 7 time-varying networks (ewma 0.97, ewma 0.94, dcc, rolling 63d, rolling 252d) beat the static (expanding full-history) network on stress days with Diebold-Mariano p < 0.05; regime (HMM) and stressed (high VIX) do worse. The best, ewma 0.97, changes the scaled prediction error of the same-day cross-section by -18% (DM t = -3.9), beats static on 73% of stress days, and lowers the error of predicted portfolio P&L by 16-30% across the five portfolios. The winners all weight recent data heavily, so they follow the current dependence structure; covariances conditioned on past stress (regime (HMM) and stressed (high VIX)) do worse, consistent with crises differing from one another (the stock-bond correlation had opposite signs in 2008-2020 and in 2022). No model is well calibrated: their nominal 90% intervals cover only 62-80% of realized stress-day moves (62% for static). Among years with at least 10 stress days, ewma 0.97 gains most in 2010, 2026 and least in 2011. The lagged network adds little: a rolling VAR predicts the day after an S&P 500 shock better than 'no further move' mainly for DXY, BAA10Y, EEM, series that absorb part of each day's S&P 500 news only the next day (late-reaction scores DXY +0.10, BAA10Y +0.09, EEM +0.11: earlier closes, stale marks or foreign underlying markets). That multi-day 'propagation' is a timing effect.
q5: Partly. On the S&P 500's worst 5% of days, 6 of 6 risky assets (EFA, EEM, XLF, HYG, USO, DBC) are more correlated with it than a Gaussian with the same overall dependence implies; under that Gaussian the correlation would shrink toward zero in the tail, so an excess is tail dependence rather than a conditioning artefact. Treasuries and the yen show the mirror image: they rally on the S&P 500's worst days more often than a Gaussian implies (crash-and-rally frequency IEF 0.32 vs 0.13, TLT 0.30 vs 0.13, FXY 0.26 vs 0.13). As forecasts, correlations measured on past tail days predict the next year's tail-day correlations with a mean absolute error of 0.257, against 0.252 for the full history and 0.234 for the last 252 days (lowest error: past calm days; past tail days beat the full history in 20% of years, DM t = 1.0). For a multi-asset portfolio's volatility on tail days the errors are 9.3% with tail correlations vs 10.9% with the full history. Crisis-correlation rises survive the Forbes-Rigobon volatility adjustment in 16 of the 30 pair-crisis cases that are significant unadjusted.
q6: No. Hedges that adapt to recent data reduce the S&P 500's variance the most: dcc 24.7% with Treasuries, gold and the dollar, and ewma 0.97 17.3% with Treasuries alone, against 9.0% and 8.0% for a static hedge. The HMM regime hedges reduce it by 6.1% and 5.6% (multi-asset), no better than static, and the best regime-based method (change-point window (BOCPD), 19.2%) trails dcc by 5.5 points (Diebold-Mariano p = 0.000); with Treasuries alone the gap is -1.6 points (p = 0.011). The HMM's value is episodic. In the 2020 crash its hedge returned -22.7% against -33.4% unhedged and -28.0% for dcc; in the 2022 rate shock it stayed long Treasuries while stocks and bonds fell together (-40.1% with a Treasury hedge vs -24.1% unhedged and -27.3% for EWMA). That pattern is consistent with its high-volatility state having been estimated on flight-to-quality crises: regime detection flags when markets are stressed, but a hedge needs the current correlation, and the regime model supplies the correlation of past crises.
